title: Fill a lidded weekly pill organizer for Monday, Wednesday and Friday
instruction: put one tablet in each of the monday, wednesday and friday compartments and close their lids
context: Filling a weekly pill organizer is a daily chore for older adults and their carers, and the hard part is physical: popping small snap lids open by a fingertip tab, dropping a 2 g caplet into a 4.6 cm cell without knocking neighbouring cells, and pressing each lid until it snaps shut. A tablet in the wrong day, a double dose or a lid left open is a medication error.
setup: Positions are measured on the table from the midpoint between the two arm bases: forward is away from the arms, left and right as seen from behind the arms. (1) Pill organizer: blue plastic, stuck to the table with putty, 35.4 cm wide, 6.8 cm deep, 2.3 cm tall; seven compartments in a row, each 4.6 cm wide and 6 cm deep inside, walls 4 mm thick and 2 cm tall on a 3 mm floor. Nominally its compartments' near inside edge is 27 cm forward and it is centred left to right, Monday's compartment centre 15 cm left, then every 5 cm to Sunday's 15 cm right; each trial moves it by a random offset of up to 3 cm forward/back and left/right and turns it by up to 15 degrees. Each compartment has its own snap lid: a light-blue plastic plate 6.8 cm deep, 4.8 cm wide and 2 mm thick (5 g), hinged along the top of the back wall, with a grip tab 2.5 cm long, 1.6 cm wide and 8 mm tall sticking out toward the arms from the middle of its front edge, and its day letter printed on top in matte black block capitals 4 cm wide and 5.6 cm tall, reading upright from behind the arms: M T W T F S S from left to right. A closed lid is held shut by a snap that takes about 1 N of lift at the tab to release and clicks shut when the lid is pressed down; once open, the stiff hinge (about 0.02 N m of friction) holds the lid at whatever angle it is left, up to 150 degrees. All seven lids start snapped shut. (2) Pill tray: a grey plastic block, 10 cm deep, 26 cm wide, 3 cm tall, fixed, centred 13 cm forward and left to right. (3) Tablets: three white caplets, 22 x 10 x 8 mm, 2 g each, lying flat on the tray with their long side pointing forward. Their nominal centres are 13 cm forward at 8 cm left, centred, and 8 cm right; each trial moves each caplet by its own random offset of up to 3 cm forward/back and left/right. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Scored once, after the episode ends. A tablet is in a compartment if it has been let go and lies on that compartment's floor: its centre inside the walls, less than 13 mm above the floor, and not moving. A lid is closed if it is snapped shut: open less than 3 degrees (its front edge less than 4 mm above the wall tops). 0.0 if any tablet is in Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday or Sunday (wrong day). Otherwise, for each of Monday, Wednesday and Friday holding exactly one tablet: 1/3 if its lid is closed, 1/6 if not; the total is rounded to two decimals (0, 0.17, 0.33, 0.5, 0.67, 0.83 or 1.0). A day holding two or three tablets (a double dose) earns nothing. Tablets anywhere else (tray, table, label strip, on a lid or a wall top, or still in the gripper) don't count. Other days' lids may be left open without penalty. Doing nothing scores 0.
reset_notes: Empty every compartment and snap all seven lids shut. Re-stick the organizer at a fresh random offset and turn and put the three caplets on the tray at their marked nominal spots, each shifted by a fresh random offset (up to 3 cm forward/back and left/right; the README gives a die-roll table). The tray stays fixed. Real 22 mm vitamin caplets or 3D-printed replicas both work; replace any that crack.
fidelity: Calibrated YAM station replica in Isaac Lab-Arena (Isaac Sim). The organizer is a 1.5 kg rigid base standing in for one stuck down with putty; its seven rigid lids have friction hinges plus a snap modelled as a 0.08 N m closing torque within 4 degrees of shut. Day letters are 1 mm raised strips on the lids. Caplets are rigid 22 x 10 x 8 mm boxes with square edges, so they settle a little differently from rounded ones.
